newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine rate spreads seen holding back growth.
newsitem.headline: Argentine rate spreads seen holding back growth.

text.p: Recent sharp improvements in Argentina's economic fundamentals have not paid off much for borrowers, who still have to pay around 11 percentage points more on their loans than they earn on their deposits in pesos.

While higher growth, falling country risk and rising domestic savings rates have shrunk the spread from the more than 300 points seen in the early 1990s, the large gap still restricts growth, analysts said.

The Argentine Bankers Association estimates average bank lending rates at 17.3 percent compared with 6.3 percent on deposits, making a difference of 11 points compared with 7.3 in Chile and less than four points in the United States.

Even though the differential has fallen by huge amounts since the end of hyperinflation in the 1980s, it is a particularly big obstacle to the growth of small and medium-sized firms that do not have access to the cheaper credit available to large companies in the international capital markets.

The AIFE study noted the gap has shrunk from 348 points in early 1991, but said: "The structural reforms, in addition to the new institutional norms, should have been sufficient to normalize and develop the financial as well as the capital markets."

The government of President Carlos Menem that came to power in 1989 has introduced far-reaching reforms of the economy, including mass privatizations and deregulation as well as "Convertibility," pegging the value of the peso to the dollar at par. Convertibility has cut inflation to less than one percent in 1996 from nearly 5,000 percent in 1989.
The Argentine Banker's Association (ABA) has put the issue of the wide spread high on the agenda at its next annual convention.

"The large difference in rates is explained by the fact that there is not perfect competition but rather a strong concentration of banking activity resembling a monopoly," said one private sector analyst who did not want to be named.

A recent report by ABA breaks down the cost of the rate of lending for the banks. It said 26 percent is due to taxes, 13 percent administration, 14 percent for bad debt provisions, 37 percent to raise the funds needed for lending and 10 percent because of minimum reserve requirements.

Another reason given by AIFE for the high rates is that there are "pockets of inefficiency in the administration at the financial entities." Administration costs takes up some 10 percent of financing at banks compared with 3.7 percent in the United States and 2.4 percent in neighboring Chile.

Analysts also blame the low levels of money circulating in the economy. One way of estimating this is the relation between M3, the broadest measure of money supply, and gross domestic product, which puts Argentina at the bottom of the scale of the major Latin American economies.

According to figures from financial consultancy Macroeconomica, Argentina has a ratio of 21.5 percent of M3 to GDP, Mexico 25.6 percent and Brazil 38.2 percent. France has 62.9 percent and Spain 80.9 percent.
Argentina's turbulent economic history goes a long way towards explaining these low levels.
The authorities have confiscated savings kept in banks until as recently as the late 1980s, something which has contributed to an estimated $70 billion being held by Argentines abroad.

Jose Rutman, an economist at consultants Broda y Asociados, points out that lending rate levels are also a consequence of banks choosing alternative places to invest their money, such as stock and bond markets.

Another factor, say analysts, is the lack of a centralized information system on borrowers, meaning it is difficult for lenders to build up records on those individuals and firms that pay their debts. This means all borrowers have to bear the cost of those who do not pay their debts.
